# 14 — Cable drive for continuous rotation: driving a wheel with a rope

*Generated by [`analysis/cable_drive_continuous.py`](../../analysis/cable_drive_continuous.py); numbers in
[`hw/cable_drive.json`](../../hw/cable_drive.json). Round 18, answering the review's question: a joint
capstan needs the cable terminated at both ends, so can a cable drive turn a wheel continuously?*

## The short answer

Yes, and for the carrier it is not even hard. **Give up the termination and a capstan becomes a rope
drive** — a friction transmission, which is what every belt has always been. The interesting part is
what you trade.

| | Terminated capstan | Rope loop, wedge groove | Toothed belt |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous rotation | **no** — 54° and it stops | yes | yes |
| Slip under overload | never | at the friction limit | never |
| Ratio in **one** stage | 20:1 | **20:1** | 6.5:1 |
| Shaft pretension, always on | none | 623 N | negligible |
| Rope / belt is a wear item | yes (unquantified) | **yes** | no, in practice |

## Why the termination is there, and why a wheel does not need it

The rope in [`analysis/capstan.py`](../../analysis/capstan.py) is anchored at both ends of the sector.
That anchor is what makes it a capstan rather than a belt: it cannot slip at any torque, and it has no
backlash, so the joint's position is a rigid function of the motor's. Both properties are bought by
giving up rotation — the drum has 3 working wraps, so at 20:1 the output gets 0.15 of a revolution.
**On a Ø160 sprocket that is 54°, or 75 mm of ground, and then it stops.**

A wheel needs neither property. It does not need zero backlash, because nothing downstream cares about
its absolute angle; and it does not need guaranteed no-slip, because the tyre or track slips against
the ground long before the transmission would. So the termination is pure cost on a drivetrain, and
dropping it is the right move rather than a compromise.

![Five architectures](platform/cable-drive-architectures.png)

## The five ways, and what each costs

**A · Terminated capstan.** What we have. 54° of wheel rotation. Not a candidate; included as the
baseline the question starts from.

**B · Endless spliced loop, round groove.** Splice the rope into a ring and it is a rope drive — the
Victorian mill transmission, and the ancestor of every V-belt. It works on the half wrap two pulleys
give you for free. Its cost is friction: Dyneema on aluminium is about μ = 0.085, which is *very* low,
so passing 253 N of tangential force needs a 1082 N tight side and puts **1910 N on the shafts
whenever the machine is switched on**, load or no load. That thick tight side needs a 2.5 mm rope,
which by the D/d ≥ 8 rule needs a Ø20 drive pulley, which spends the ratio down to 12:1.

**C · Endless loop in a 36° wedge groove.** The wedge multiplies effective friction by 1/sin(β/2), so
μ' = 0.28. This is the one non-obvious result in the study, because the benefit compounds three ways:

1. shaft pretension falls from 1910 N to **623 N**;
2. the lower tight side lets a **1.5 mm** rope carry it instead of 2.5 mm — 11× lighter per metre;
3. a 1.5 mm rope may run on a **Ø12** pulley at D/d 8, which takes the single-stage ratio to **20:1**.

**Rope diameter and pulley diameter are one decision, not two**, and the groove shape sits upstream of
both. This is the elevator traction sheave, which has done exactly this job — continuous rotation,
friction only, undercut grooves to raise effective μ — for a century.

**D · Toothed belt.** Worth saying plainly: **a toothed belt is a cable drive.** Its tension member is
cord; the teeth are how it solved termination, and the elastomer around the cord is how it solved the
wear problem below. Gates' smallest stock 8MGT sprocket is 22 grooves (Ø56.0 mm), so one stage stops
at 6.5:1 and reaching 20:1 takes two stages, two shafts and two sets of bearings.

**E · Two terminated capstans with one-way clutches.** Rectify a reciprocating stroke into continuous
rotation and you keep the no-slip and the zero backlash. It is a real mechanism, and it is the wrong
one here: at 20:1 each stroke is 0.15 output revolutions, so the carrier needs **13,263 full rope
load-reversals per kilometre**, the output torque pulses at the stroke rate, and reversing needs
switchable rather than one-way clutches.

## What it costs, honestly

![The trade](platform/cable-drive-tradeoff.png)

**The rope becomes a wear item.** Every element of an endless loop is bent once at each pulley on every
circuit, which for this geometry is **2,885 bend cycles per kilometre driven**. Published
bend-over-sheave lives for bare HMPE braid near its working load sit in the 10³–10⁴ band, which if it
transfers means **0.3 to 3.5 km per rope**. Even taking that as 100× pessimistic for a lightly loaded
1.5 mm braid, it is 35–350 km against the ~2,000 km of transit a carrier should do in a season.

That band is order-of-magnitude and comes from a page this VM could not open (`marlowropes.com` serves
a CAPTCHA; recorded as blocked in [`docs/reference/manifest.yaml`](../reference/manifest.yaml)), measured
on large offshore ropes. **It sizes the gap; it does not close it.** Nothing should be built on it —
the number has to be measured on the real rope, groove and load.

**And the gap the question exposed in work already done:** the same calculation says the *walking leg's*
capstan rope sees **2,500 bend cycles per kilometre walked** — the drivetrain is not the outlier. The
rope this project accepted eight rounds ago has the same problem and **its life was never computed**.
That is a real hole in §8, not a new objection to §14.

Two smaller costs: elastic creep of order 1 % is inherent to any friction drive, putting about **5 W**
into the rope at peak against its **80 °C** critical temperature (Marlow datasheet) — comfortable here,
but it scales with torque and would not stay comfortable on a bigger machine. And SK78 creeps 0.5 %/yr
at 20 % load, so an endless loop needs a spring tensioner rather than a set length.

## What this means for the carrier

The carrier's drivetrain is a **low-torque** application, which is what makes all of this easy: 9 N·m at
the sprocket on the level, 30 N·m pulling away on a 30° slope, 143 rpm at 1.2 m/s. The $50 8318 from the
round-11 market search needs 11.6:1 minimum and runs at 2,865 rpm of its 4,800 no-load at 20:1.

So the recommendation is:

1. **Use a toothed belt unless you need more than 6.5:1 in one stage.** It is the same idea with the
   cord protected, and that protection is exactly what buys the life the bare rope cannot show.
2. **If the single-stage ratio matters** — a sealed hull with one thin element crossing to the wheel,
   no intermediate shaft, no second bearing pair — then the wedge-groove rope loop is the right answer,
   and it must be designed as a **serviceable wear item**: a spring tensioner, a route you can reach
   without dismantling the drive, and a spliced loop cheap enough to carry spares of.
3. **Do not build the clutch-pair.** It preserves a property the wheel does not need, at the price of
   13,000 rope reversals per kilometre.
4. **Note what a track already is.** On a tracked carrier the continuous tension loop is the track
   itself; the rope drive is only earning its place between the motor and the sprocket.

## What is computed and what is assumed

Computed: sprocket torque and speed from the marsupial study's own mass and cost of transport; the
tight/slack tensions and shaft loads from Euler-Eytelwein; rope diameter from the datasheet's d² scaling
at the safety factor `analysis/capstan.py` already uses; drive-pulley diameter from D/d ≥ 8; the ratio
that leaves; loop length and bend cycles per kilometre from geometry alone, with no fatigue curve in them.

Assumed, and sensitive: the Ø160 drive sprocket and Ø240 driven pulley (both chosen, not derived); the
300 mm centre distance; the 30° gradeability requirement, which nobody has written down as a
requirement; the 36° groove angle; and 1 % creep loss. **μ = 0.085 is unconfirmed**, so the figure sweeps
it from 0.05 to 0.25 and no conclusion rests on the single value — the wedge groove wins across the whole
sweep. The rope-life band is the weakest number in the study and is flagged everywhere it is used.
